feedback.correct: The leaf needs light energy, water and carbon dioxide together to make food. With light blocked, no new food is made, so growth stops and the plants decline even though water and carbon dioxide are supplied.
feedback.incorrect: Water and carbon dioxide are two of the three inputs, but the leaf also needs light energy. options.text: Growth will be poor because the plants cannot use water and carbon dioxide to make food without light energy from the sun.
Growth will be normal because the plants get enough water and carbon dioxide, which are the two things they need to make food.
Growth will be normal because the plants can absorb ready-made food from the soil as long as water is present.
Growth will be poor only if the greenhouse also becomes too cool, since light mainly matters for warmth.

option_notes.b: Water and carbon dioxide alone are not enough; light energy is also needed for the leaf to make food.

display.body: **Inside the leaf, light energy joins water and carbon dioxide to make sugar — the plant's own food — and oxygen is released.**
display.title: Key idea

accessibility.description: Key idea: inside the leaf, light energy joins water and carbon dioxide to make sugar, the plant's food, and oxygen is released.

display.text: Inside the leaf, light energy drives a joining reaction. Water and carbon dioxide are bonded together into **sugar**, the plant's food, and **oxygen** is released as the sugar forms. The energy held in that sugar is the light energy the leaf absorbed. The plant builds this food itself, using captured energy rather than energy it creates.

accessibility.description: Explanation that light energy drives water and carbon dioxide to join into sugar inside the leaf, that oxygen is released, that the sugar holds the light energy the leaf absorbed, and that the plant makes this food itself.

display.caption: Light energy arriving at the leaf, water arriving at the leaf and carbon dioxide arriving at the leaf. Inside the leaf, light energy, water and carbon dioxide joined to make food (sugar), with oxygen released as the food is made.

items: The **sugar** made in the leaf leaves the leaf and is carried to the parts of the plant that are growing, such as new leaves, the stem and the roots.
There the sugar is used to build new plant material, and that is why the plant gets bigger over time.
Some of the sugar is not used straight away; it is stored in the plant for later use, and the energy kept in that store is the light energy the leaf captured.
This is what the windowsill plant was doing: making sugar in its leaves, then using or storing it. The cupboard plant, whose leaf receives no light energy, builds no new food at all.

accessibility.description: Ordered sequence following the sugar the leaf makes: it leaves the leaf, is carried to growing parts, is used to build new plant material so the plant grows, and some is stored for later use holding the captured light energy; the windowsill plant was doing this, while the cupboard plant builds no new food.

display.text:
**Two plants that differ in only one way can end up looking nothing alike.**

These two plants are the same kind and the same size. They were planted in the same soil, in the same sort of pot, and watered the same amount on the same days. The only difference between them was the light: one sat on a sunny windowsill, the other in a dark cupboard.

After two weeks the windowsill plant was green and taller, with new growth. The cupboard plant was pale, limp and had produced no new growth at all. The cupboard plant had the same soil and the same water, so what was the light doing for the windowsill plant?

accessibility.description: A matched pair of plants described: same kind, same size, same soil and pot, watered the same amount on the same days, and differing only in the light each received. After two weeks the windowsill plant is green and taller while the cupboard plant is pale, limp and has no new growth, leaving the question of what the light was doing for the windowsill plant.

display.text:
A plant takes in three things: *water*, *carbon dioxide* and *light energy*. It needs all three of them. Before we go further, remind yourself where each one reaches the plant. Which part takes water out of the soil? Where does carbon dioxide come from? Which part catches the light?

Hold on to those three routes, because the next step is to look at what happens where all three arrive.

accessibility.description: A prompt to recall that a plant takes in water, carbon dioxide and light energy, and to remember for yourself where each one reaches the plant: which part takes water from the soil, where carbon dioxide comes from, and which part catches the light.

items: Name the three inputs a leaf needs to make food: light energy, water and carbon dioxide.
For each plant, check whether each of those three inputs is actually reaching the leaf.
Flag any input that is blocked or no longer arriving, and say which one it is.
Then decide whether that leaf can make food, and give the missing input with your answer.

accessibility.description: Four ordered steps for judging each plant: list the leaf's three inputs, check which ones reach the leaf, note any missing input, then decide whether food can be made.

display.text:
**The three inputs are not alternatives: water, carbon dioxide and light energy must all reach the leaf together for food to be made.**

It is tempting to treat light energy, water and carbon dioxide as a checklist where two out of three will do. That reading fails, because the food is built by joining water and carbon dioxide, and light energy is what drives that joining. Take away any single one and the joining cannot happen, so no sugar is built.

When carbon dioxide cannot reach the leaf, there is nothing for the water to join, so no sugar is built even though light energy and water keep arriving. When water does not arrive, the same joining has nothing to work with, so no sugar forms even though light energy and carbon dioxide are both present.

In each case two inputs are there, yet the single missing one stops food-making. A plant missing one input does not stop the moment it is taken away. It keeps drawing on food it made earlier and stored, so it fades over days rather than halting at once. That slow decline is why the missing input is easy to overlook.

accessibility.description: Explanation that water, carbon dioxide and light energy must all be present in the leaf together; if any one is missing, the joining that builds sugar cannot happen, and the plant only fades over days because it lives on stored food in the meantime.

source_facts.text: Light energy arriving at the leaf, water arriving at the leaf and carbon dioxide arriving at the leaf. Inside the leaf, light energy, water and carbon dioxide joined to make food (sugar), with oxygen released as the food is made.
Key idea **Inside the leaf, light energy joins water and carbon dioxide to make sugar — the plant's own food — and oxygen is released.**
Inside the leaf, light energy drives a joining reaction.

display.text:
**Two plants grown side by side, differing in one thing only, show us what that one thing does.**

Both plants were the same kind and the same size, planted in the same soil in the same sort of pot. They were watered the same amount on the same days. One stood on a sunny windowsill; the other sat in a dark cupboard.

After two weeks the windowsill plant was green and taller. The cupboard plant was pale and limp, and had produced no new growth. The cupboard plant had the same soil and the same water, so what was the light doing for the windowsill plant?

accessibility.description: An opening comparison of two plants of the same kind, soil, pot and watering, where only light differed: one on a sunny windowsill grew green and taller, while one in a dark cupboard turned pale, limp and made no new growth. The paragraph ends on the open question of what the light was doing for the windowsill plant.

items: **Water** reaches the plant through its **roots**, which take it in from the soil; the stem then carries it up to the leaves.
**Carbon dioxide** reaches the leaves from the air around the plant, passing in through small **openings** in the leaf surface.
**Light energy** reaches the leaves from the sun, and the leaves **absorb** it.
A plant needs all three — water, carbon dioxide and light — and it fails to grow well when any one of them is missing.

accessibility.description: A list recalling the route of each of the three inputs a plant takes in: water through the roots from the soil, carried up the stem to the leaves; carbon dioxide from the air through small openings in the leaves; and light energy from the sun, absorbed by the leaves. The list ends by noting a plant needs all three.

display.title: “Light just keeps the plant warm”
display.belief: The light coming through the window only warms the plant. It is that warmth that keeps a plant healthy, and a warm sunny windowsill is why my plant grows so well.
display.evidence: The cupboard plant sat in the same room, so it was no colder than the windowsill plant — only darker. If warmth were what mattered, it would have thrived. Instead it built no new food and did not grow.
display.conclusion: Light is an energy input the leaf uses to make food; the energy stored in the sugar is light energy, not warmth. Warmth without light gives the plant no energy to make food.

accessibility.description: Misconception callout: the belief that light only warms a plant, tested by the cupboard plant, which was warm but dark and still built no new food and did not grow.

display.title: “The soil is the plant’s food”
display.belief: The plant's food comes ready-made from the soil. The soil feeds it, and the water I pour on is part of that food.
display.evidence: The cupboard plant had exactly the same soil and exactly the same water as the windowsill plant. If soil and water were its food, it should have grown just as well — and it did not.
display.conclusion: The soil supplies water and minerals only, not food. The plant makes its own food in the leaf from water and carbon dioxide using light energy, so nothing is taken ready-made from the soil.

accessibility.description: Misconception callout: the belief that soil and water are the plant's ready-made food, tested by two plants with identical soil and water where only the dark one failed, showing the soil supplies water and minerals only.

display.body: **Inside the leaf, light energy joins water and carbon dioxide to make sugar, the plant's food, and oxygen is released.**
display.aside: The plant builds this food itself, inside its leaves.

accessibility.description: Key idea callout: inside the leaf, light energy joins water and carbon dioxide to make sugar, the plant's food, and oxygen is released.

display.caption: Light energy arriving at the leaf, water arriving at the leaf and carbon dioxide arriving at the leaf meet at the same place — the leaf. There, light energy, water and carbon dioxide joined inside the leaf to make food (sugar), and oxygen released as the food is made. The energy now held in the food (sugar) is the light energy the leaf took in.

display.text:
The **sugar** made in the leaf does not stay there. It is carried to the parts that are growing — new leaves, stem and roots — and used there to build new plant material, which is why the plant gets bigger. Some of the sugar is not used straight away but is stored, holding the light energy the leaf captured.

The windowsill plant was doing just this: making food in its leaves, using it to grow and storing some. The cupboard plant sits in darkness; its leaf receives no light energy, so it builds no new food at all.

accessibility.description: Paragraph tracing where the sugar goes: it is carried to growing new leaves, stem and roots and used to build new plant material, some is stored for later use, and the windowsill plant did this while the cupboard plant receives no light energy and builds no food.

Then check **carbon dioxide** — can air reach the leaf openings, or is the leaf coated so air cannot get in?

accessibility.description: An ordered three-step check for inspecting a plant: light energy reaching the leaf, then water from the soil, then carbon dioxide entering through the leaf openings.

display.aside: A plant that loses an input does not stop at once. New food is no longer made, so it lives on what it made earlier and stored, fading over days rather than halting on the spot.
display.title: Two out of three is not enough
display.belief: As long as light and one other input reach the leaf, it can keep making food — the third input only matters if the other two run short.
display.evidence: Keep light energy and one other input reaching the leaf, and stop only the third — block the leaf openings so carbon dioxide cannot enter, or withhold water. If the inputs worked independently, food-making would continue.
display.conclusion: Water, carbon dioxide and light energy are not alternatives: the leaf needs all three at the same time, and if any one is missing, no food is made.

accessibility.description: Callout correcting the belief that two of the three inputs are enough. It asks the learner to test that belief by stopping only one input, then states that water, carbon dioxide and light energy must all be present together, and notes that a plant draws on stored food before it visibly declines.

display.title: “Light just keeps the plant warm”
display.belief: The light coming through the window only warms the plant. It is that warmth that keeps a plant healthy, and a warm sunny windowsill is why my plant grows so well.
display.evidence: The cupboard plant sat in the same room, so it was no colder than the windowsill plant — only darker. If warmth were what mattered, it would have thrived. Instead it built no new food and did not grow.
display.conclusion: Light is an energy input the leaf uses to make food; the energy stored in the sugar is light energy, not warmth. Warmth without light gives the plant no energy to make food.

accessibility.description: Misconception callout: the belief that light only warms a plant, tested by the cupboard plant, which was warm but dark and still built no new food and did not grow.

display.title: “The soil is the plant’s food”
display.belief: The plant's food comes ready-made from the soil. The soil feeds it, and the water I pour on is part of that food.
display.evidence: The cupboard plant had exactly the same soil and exactly the same water as the windowsill plant. If soil and water were its food, it should have grown just as well — and it did not.
display.conclusion: The soil supplies water and minerals only, not food. The plant makes its own food in the leaf from water and carbon dioxide using light energy, so nothing is taken ready-made from the soil.

accessibility.description: Misconception callout: the belief that soil and water are the plant's ready-made food, tested by two plants with identical soil and water where only the dark one failed, showing the soil supplies water and minerals only.
